text: Type 2 Diabetes
explanation_or_correction: Draft educational reference: MedlinePlus, https://medlineplus.gov/diabetestype2.html. Course-specific guideline and teaching level to be confirmed with Lavin.

text: Glucose and insulin basics: Glucose as an energy source; the role of insulin in helping glucose enter body cells.
Which statement about insulin is correct?
option_A: Insulin helps glucose move from the blood into cells
option_B: Insulin is a hormone produced by the lungs
option_D: Insulin normally keeps glucose out of body cells
explanation_or_correction: Insulin helps blood glucose enter cells where it can be used for energy.

text: Where does much of the body's glucose come from?
explanation_or_correction: Glucose comes largely from the foods we eat.

text: Which description best fits high blood glucose?
option_A: The body has stopped making energy completely
option_B: All glucose has disappeared from cells
option_C: Too much glucose remains in the bloodstream
explanation_or_correction: When insulin is insufficient or less effective, blood glucose may remain high.

text: Insulin normally raises blood sugar by keeping glucose out of cells.
explanation_or_correction: Insulin helps glucose enter cells and generally lowers the amount of glucose remaining in blood.

text: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes: Cells' reduced response to insulin, compensatory insulin production and rising blood glucose.
What is insulin resistance?
option_A: Having no blood glucose at all
option_B: A sudden infection of the pancreas
option_C: The body produces no insulin at all
option_D: Cells not responding normally to insulin
explanation_or_correction: With insulin resistance, cells do not respond to insulin as effectively.

text: What may happen when the body's insulin response becomes less effective?
option_A: The pancreas may initially make more insulin
option_D: Insulin is no longer a hormone
explanation_or_correction: The body may compensate by making more insulin, but blood glucose can eventually rise.

text: Which statement about type 2 diabetes is most accurate?
option_B: It involves the body's difficulty using insulin effectively, sometimes with insufficient insulin production
option_C: It is diagnosed by counting the number of meals eaten
option_D: It is always caused by eating one sugary food
explanation_or_correction: Type 2 diabetes often involves insulin resistance and reduced ability to maintain normal glucose levels.

text: Insulin resistance means the body has no insulin at all.
explanation_or_correction: In insulin resistance, cells respond less well to insulin; the body may still produce insulin.

text: Risk factors and prevention: Family history, physical activity and other modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors.
Which statement about type 2 diabetes risk is accurate?
option_A: Only one factor can ever affect risk
option_B: Only people with a family history can develop type 2 diabetes
option_C: Family history can increase risk, but diabetes can also occur without it
option_D: Everyone has exactly the same risk
explanation_or_correction: Family history is one recognized risk factor, though it is not necessary for diabetes to develop.

text: Which is an example of a modifiable risk factor?
explanation_or_correction: Activity levels can be modified, unlike age or inherited risk.

text: Why should a person with several risk factors ask about screening?
option_A: To establish whether testing is appropriate even when symptoms are absent
option_B: Because a risk factor always means they have diabetes
option_C: Because screening replaces all follow-up care
option_D: Because they can determine diagnosis from family history alone
explanation_or_correction: Risk factors can guide a healthcare professional's decision about appropriate screening.

text: Only people with a family history can develop type 2 diabetes.
explanation_or_correction: Family history can raise risk, but it is not required for type 2 diabetes to develop.

text: Monitoring and complications: Why glucose is monitored and why long-term high blood glucose can affect organs.
Which statement about glucose monitoring is accurate?
option_A: Feeling well always means monitoring is unnecessary
option_B: Monitoring helps show glucose trends and support management discussions
option_D: One measurement replaces every clinical review
explanation_or_correction: Glucose measurements help individuals and care teams evaluate management over time.

text: Which body systems can be affected by prolonged high blood glucose?
option_C: Blood vessels, nerves, kidneys and eyes
explanation_or_correction: Long-term high blood glucose can affect blood vessels, nerves and several organs.

text: Why might a clinician review a pattern of readings rather than only one number?
option_A: All readings are identical throughout the day
option_B: One high number always confirms a complication
option_C: A reading cannot be affected by daily conditions
option_D: Trends over time provide more context than an isolated measurement
explanation_or_correction: Blood glucose changes over time; patterns can help guide clinical decisions.

text: Feeling well proves that blood glucose is within the target range.
explanation_or_correction: High blood glucose can occur without noticeable symptoms; monitoring and professional guidance matter.

text: Self-management and professional follow-up: Everyday self-management, following an individualized care plan and checking treatment changes with a care team.
Which action supports safe diabetes self-management?
option_A: Following an agreed care plan and discussing changes with the care team
option_C: Changing medicine doses based on an online quiz
option_D: Stopping prescribed diabetes treatment as soon as symptoms improve
explanation_or_correction: Self-management includes following a personalized plan and reviewing changes with healthcare professionals.

text: Which approach is best for learning how lifestyle factors affect glucose?
option_B: Record relevant patterns and discuss them with the healthcare team
option_C: Assume everyone should follow the same plan
explanation_or_correction: Tracking relevant patterns can inform individualized care conversations.

text: What should a student conclude from a fictional class case where glucose is repeatedly above a prescribed target?
option_A: A diagnosis and dose can be selected from the quiz alone
option_B: The record has no educational value
option_C: The pattern should be reviewed in the context of an individualized clinical care plan
option_D: The patient should skip every meal
explanation_or_correction: A pattern should be interpreted in a clinical context; education questions do not give individual treatment directions.

text: A person should change or stop prescribed diabetes treatment as soon as symptoms improve.
explanation_or_correction: Changes to prescribed diabetes care should be discussed with the treating healthcare professional.
